extracted.intended_audience: readers of an 18th-century periodical (general literate public)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting prescriptive principles and evaluative maxims embedded in an 18th-century periodical/moral essay (The Adventurer). The page offers guidance on industry, hope, belief, and the nature and giving of advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligent labour deserves sustenance
rubrics_metrics.description: "he that will diligently labour, in whatever occupation, will deserve the sustenance which he obtains, and the protection which he enjoys; and may lie down every night with the pleasing consciousness of having contributed something to the happiness of life."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation and examples throughout the essay: even seemingly despicable or minute occupations support people; custom and diverse tastes create demand for many arts so that industry of all sorts prevents idleness and want. The passage defends the moral and social value of steady labour in any form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do the little you can without delay
rubrics_metrics.description: "no man is without some quality, by the due application of which he might deserve well of the world; and whoever he be that has but little in his power, should be in haste to do that little, lest he be confounded with him that can do nothing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages prompt use of whatever small abilities or resources one possesses; a practical injunction against apathy and against hiding behind excuses of having little to contribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief ought to be proportioned to evidence or probability
rubrics_metrics.description: "We are all ready to confess, that belief ought to be proportioned to evidence or probability."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay recommends comparing rare lucky successes to the numerous failures to judge one's own odds honestly. It uses examples (e.g., Tom Drowsy) to show how self-delusion about projects is exposed when tested against public scrutiny or probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test schemes by explainability to others
rubrics_metrics.description: "Whatever is true will bear to be related, whatever is rational will endure to be explained; but when we delight to brood in secret over future happiness... we are cheating ourselves by voluntary delusions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical test for the reasonableness of plans: prepare to explain the project/minute particulars to others. If the project cannot withstand explanation or would provoke derision when stated plainly, it is likely folly. The Tom Drowsy anecdote illustrates that schemes that seem convincing to their originator often collapse when exposed for external evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hope is useful in moderation but dangerous in excess
rubrics_metrics.description: "these pleasures, like the rest, are lawful only in certain circumstances, and to certain degrees; they may be useful in a due subserviency to nobler purposes, but become dangerous and destructive when once they gain the ascendant in the heart... to lull our faculties in a lethargy is poor and despicable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hope can invigorate and help sustain effort in difficult circumstances, but excessive hope that replaces action leads to idleness and ruin. The essay balances allowance for consolatory hope with warnings against its intoxicating, paralysing excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advice (as used here) should be prudential, not absolute moral doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: "By advice I would not be understood to mean, the everlasting and invariable principles of moral and religious truth... but such directions as respect merely the prudential part of conduct, and which may be followed or neglected without any violation of essential duties."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the scope of 'advice' treated in the essay: practical, prudential guidance aimed at making people wiser about conduct, distinct from immutable moral or religious laws. This delineation frames what kinds of counsel the author discusses and recommends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective advice requires a willing listener and skillful delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: "since advice cannot be given but to those that will hear it, a patient listener is necessary to the accommodation of all those who desire to be confirmed in the opinion of their own wisdom... good counsel is only thrown away upon those who are full of their own perfections."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Twofold criterion: (1) advice must be offered to someone willing to hear; (2) manner of giving advice matters—unskilful or nauseous delivery will cause rejection even if the counsel is sound. The text gives social examples (favor shown to a docile niece, bequests influenced by docility) to illustrate practical effects of receptiveness and manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break large tasks into daily parts and act each day
rubrics_metrics.description: "whatever can be completed in a year, is divisible into parts, of which each may be performed in the compass of a day; he, therefore, that has passed the day without attention to the task assigned him, may be certain, that the lapse of life has brought him no nearer to his object."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A procedural principle for making progress: long-term projects are achievable by consistent daily effort; idleness or failure to work daily leaves one no nearer one's goal despite the passage of time. Used to argue against relying on vague hopes and for disciplined, segmented labour.
